analysis.one_liner: Creates a consumer protection office inside the Department of Transportation to enforce rules for travelers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Schatz with six Democratic cosponsors, never left the Senate Commerce Committee and died at the end of the 118th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would establish an Office of Consumer Protection in the Department of Transportation, led by a new Assistant Secretary. The office would help travelers and shipping customers, investigate and enforce consumer protection, civil rights, and licensing rules across the transportation system, and write new consumer and civil rights regulations where needed. It would also publish an annual public report on consumer problems and trends. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers, cruise and bus riders, rail passengers, trucking and freight customers, and people who face transportation discrimination would gain a dedicated federal office to handle complaints, investigate violations, and enforce existing rules — an enforcement home that the Department of Transportation currently lacks as a single focus.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a permanent Office of Consumer Protection in DOT whose mission is to assist, educate, and protect consumers, and to investigate and enforce consumer protection, civil rights, and licensing requirements. [S2] [S3]

The office could write new consumer protection and civil rights regulations, giving DOT authority to address problems like fees, service failures, and discrimination across airlines, railroads, buses, and other modes. [S2] [S3]
The office would be led by a Senate-confirmed Assistant Secretary for Consumer Protection, putting consumer issues at a senior decision-making level rather than scattered among existing offices. [S3]
An annual public report to Congress would document consumer protection trends and major challenges facing consumers, creating public visibility and pressure. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Transportation companies — airlines, railroads, bus lines, cruise and shipping operators, and motor carriers — would bear the cost of stricter investigations, enforcement actions, and possible new regulations. Federal taxpayers would fund the new office and its staff. Some enforcement costs could be passed through to consumers in prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes a new federal office and a new Senate-confirmed assistant secretary without specifying funding, adding bureaucracy and payroll costs on top of consumer protection work DOT offices already perform, with potential overlap or duplication. [S3]

Stronger investigation and rulemaking powers over carriers could raise compliance costs for airlines, railroads, and freight companies, which may be passed to consumers as higher fares and shipping prices; supporters would counter that enforcement against unfair fees and discrimination is worth that cost. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest in design: a dedicated enforcement office and public reporting would likely improve accountability for travelers, a group with little individual power against large carriers. The main costs are a new bureaucracy of unspecified size and possible compliance costs passed to consumers. The bill is light on detail — no funding, staffing levels, or enforcement penalties — so its practical impact depends heavily on how the office were run.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, with five Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Welch, Luján, Fetterman, Markey, and Cortez Masto. [S3] [S4]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction. [S1] [S5]
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history — and the bill expired with the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Transportation companies that would have faced a dedicated DOT enforcement office are better off, since the bill never advanced; travelers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a DOT Office of Consumer Protection.

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Senate Democratic cosponsors (Welch, Luján, Fetterman, Markey, Cortez Masto plus Schatz)

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill stalled in committee without any recorded floor position.

industries.note: A dedicated DOT consumer office would investigate and enforce rules on airlines, which face recurring complaints over refunds, fees, and service failures. Their interest in weak enforcement runs against travelers' interest in redress.

The office would enforce licensing, consumer protection, and civil rights requirements across rail and motor carriers, raising compliance and enforcement exposure. Carriers benefit from the current patchwork enforcement DOT can provide.

industries.industry: Bus lines, cruise lines, and other passenger carriers
industries.note: These modes are within DOT's jurisdiction and would face a new investigative and rulemaking watchdog. Passengers currently have limited recourse against them.
